title: A special-fibre point of an etale DVR algebra has a principal DVR neighbourhood
statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_R$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Let $B$ be a commutative ring and $\varphi:R\to B$ a ring homomorphism such that $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is etale [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-etale-morphism]. Let $\mathfrak q\subset B$ be a prime ideal with $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak m_R$. There is an element $b\in B\setminus\mathfrak q$ such that $R\prime=B[1/b]$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] is a discrete valuation ring, its unique maximal ideal is $\mathfrak qB[1/b]$, and the composite $R\to B\to R\prime$ is injective and local (the inverse image of its maximal ideal is $\mathfrak m_R$). The induced morphism $\operatorname{Spec}R\prime\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is etale. No finiteness of $B$ as an $R$-module, excellence, henselianity or completeness is assumed.

source.place: Tag 0AP2, lemma-Dedekind-etale-extension, applied over the closed point of a DVR; principal-neighbourhood consequence used in models.tex lemma-etale-local-at-worst-nodal, third proof paragraph. The closed-fibre condition excludes field factors.

proof.text: Put $X=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$. First $S$ has exactly the two points $(0)$ and $\mathfrak m_R$. Indeed, $(0)$ is prime because $R$ is a domain. If a nonzero prime is $(a)$, then $a\ne0$ and $a$ is not a unit. For any proper ideal $(d)$ containing $(a)$ write $a=de$. Primality gives $d\in(a)$ or $e\in(a)$. The first alternative gives $(d)=(a)$; in the second, writing $e=ac$ and cancelling $a$ gives $dc=1$, contradicting properness. Thus every nonzero prime is maximal, and localness makes it $\mathfrak m_R$.

source.place: Tag 00PD, lemma-characterize-dvr; elementary consequence of the local PID definition

proof.text: For either $s\in S$, the scheme-theoretic fibre $X_s$ is affine by the affine fibre-product theorem, and therefore quasi-compact. The etale-fibre theorem says its underlying space is discrete. Covering this space by its open singletons and taking a finite subcover shows that $|X_s|$ is finite. The first fibre projection identifies $|X_s|$ with the set-theoretic fibre in $X$. Since $S$ has just two points, $|X|$, equivalently the set of prime ideals of $B$, is finite. This proves the quasi-local finiteness needed for the principal-neighbourhood argument without assuming $B$ finite as an $R$-module.

source.place: Tag 0CDD, lemma-etale-local-at-worst-nodal, third proof paragraph; finiteness expanded with Morphisms Tag 02GL and Algebra Tag 00E8

proof.text: Let $T$ be the finite set of prime ideals $\mathfrak p\subset B$ not contained in $\mathfrak q$. For each $\mathfrak p\in T$ choose $c_{\mathfrak p}\in\mathfrak p\setminus\mathfrak q$, and set $b=\prod_{\mathfrak p\in T}c_{\mathfrak p}$, with empty product $1$. Primality of $\mathfrak q$ gives $b\notin\mathfrak q$. Every prime in $T$ contains $b$, while no prime contained in $\mathfrak q$ contains $b$. Consequently the primes not containing $b$ are exactly the primes contained in $\mathfrak q$. This is the explicit finite prime-avoidance calculation used to shrink around the chosen point.

source.place: Tag 0CDD, lemma-etale-local-at-worst-nodal, third proof paragraph: standard open obtained by prime avoidance

proof.text: Set $C=B[1/b]$ and $\lambda:B\to C$. Apply the localization prime correspondence to the powers of $b$. The ideal $\mathfrak qC$ is prime and contracts to $\mathfrak q$; every prime of $C$ is $\mathfrak pC$ for a prime $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak q$, so it is contained in $\mathfrak qC$. Every proper ideal of $C$ is contained in a maximal ideal. Applying this first to $\mathfrak qC$ shows it is maximal; applying the containment just proved to any maximal ideal shows that it equals $\mathfrak qC$. Thus $C$ is local with unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak qC$.

proof.text:
The canonical homomorphism $\alpha:C	o B_{\mathfrak q}$ sends $x/b^n$ to the same fraction. For $s
otin\mathfrak q$, contraction of $\mathfrak qC$ implies $\lambda(s)
otin\mathfrak qC$, so the local unit criterion makes $\lambda(s)$ invertible. Hence each fraction $r/s$ in $B_{\mathfrak q}$ is the image of $\lambda(r)\lambda(s)^{-1}$: $\alpha$ is surjective. If $\alpha(x/b^n)=0$, the definition of prime localization supplies $s
otin\mathfrak q$ with $sx=0$ in $B$. Multiplication by the unit $\lambda(s)$ then shows $x/b^n=0$ in $C$, proving injectivity. The fraction formulas make $\alpha$ a $B$-algebra isomorphism. An element $x/b^n$ belongs to $\mathfrak qC$ exactly when $x\in\mathfrak q$, so $\alpha$ carries this ideal onto $\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q}$.

source.place: Tags 00CO, definition-localization, and 00E3, lemma-spec-localization; explicit fraction calculation

proof.text: Choose a uniformizer $\pi$ of $R$. The point $\mathfrak q\in X$ maps to the closed point $\mathfrak m_R$ by hypothesis. The etale trait stalk theorem therefore applies to the actual stalk $A=\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak q}$: $A$ is a DVR and the canonical map $R\to A$ is injective. The affine stalk localization theorem identifies $B_{\mathfrak q}\cong A$ by $r/s\mapsto r_{\mathfrak q}s_{\mathfrak q}^{-1}$, so this identification respects the structural map from $R$. Composing it with $\alpha$ gives an $R$-algebra isomorphism $C\cong A$. Thus $C$ is a DVR and $R\to C$ is injective. Finally $\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak qC)=\mathfrak q$, so the inverse image of the unique maximal ideal of $C$ under $R\to C$ is $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak m_R$: the map is local.

source.place: Tag 0AP2, lemma-Dedekind-etale-extension, at a prime over the closed point; Schemes Tag 01HV, lemma-spec-sheaves (6)

proof.text: The principal-localization open-immersion theorem identifies the morphism $\operatorname{Spec}C\to X$ induced by $B\to C$ as an open immersion with image $D(b)$. Open immersions are etale, and composites of etale morphisms are etale. Composing with the given $X\to S$ proves that the morphism induced by $R\to C$ is etale. Taking $R\prime=C$ now gives all the required clauses, with $b\notin\mathfrak q$ supplied by step 3.
